_note: The Ranger Journal in the 3D animal viewer: where each animal lives (home), a few true facts (facts), and how to help (help, optional). For Mythics, the legend and the real-world clue behind it (animals.json "legend" shows below). Short and friendly: read by kids.

raccoon.home: Forests, marshes and cities across North America.
facts: A raccoon's front paws are super sensitive. It feels its food all over before eating, and wet paws feel even better, which is why it seems to wash its food.
The black mask round its eyes may help cut down glare, like a football player's eye black.
raccoon.help: Keep trash cans closed so raccoons find real food, not junk.

gray_squirrel.home: Woods and parks in eastern North America.
facts: A gray squirrel buries thousands of nuts each fall. It forgets some of them, and those grow into new trees.
It can turn its back feet right round, so it can run down a tree head first.
gray_squirrel.help: Leave some old trees standing: squirrels nest in their hollows.

red_fox.home: Forests, fields and towns across the northern half of the world.
facts: No other wild meat-eater lives across so much of the world.
A fox can hear a mouse moving under the snow, then leap high and dive in nose first to catch it.
On cold nights it curls its bushy tail round itself like a blanket.

peregrine_falcon.home: Cliffs and skyscrapers on every continent except Antarctica.
facts: The fastest animal on Earth: diving after prey, a peregrine can top 320 km/h (200 mph).
Peregrines nearly vanished because of a pesticide called DDT. Once it was banned, they came back, and many now nest on tall city buildings.
Wild boars are the wild relatives of farm pigs.
Their strong snouts dig up roots, nuts and bugs, turning over the forest floor.
Baby boars have stripes, like a watermelon, to hide among the leaves.

wolf_pack.home: Forests, mountains and Arctic tundra across the north.
facts: A wolf pack is a family: two parents and their pups of different ages.
A howl can carry for about 10 km (6 miles), calling the pack together.
Wolves came back to Yellowstone Park in 1995, and scientists think they helped trees grow back along its rivers.

brown_bear.home: Forests and mountains of North America, Europe and Asia.
facts: Grizzly bears are brown bears. Their sense of smell is one of the best of any animal.
They eat berries, roots, grass and salmon, then sleep through the winter in a den.
Cubs are born in the winter den, tiny and blind, while their mother sleeps.
Hippos spend the hot day in the water and come out at night to graze on grass.
Their skin makes a reddish oily liquid that works like sunscreen.
Hippos can't really swim: they walk and bounce along the bottom.
hippopotamus.help: Hippos are Vulnerable. Protecting rivers protects them.

lion.home: Grasslands and open woods in Africa, plus one forest in India.
facts: Lions are the only cats that live in big family groups, called prides.
A lion's roar can be heard about 8 km (5 miles) away.
The lionesses do most of the hunting, working as a team.
lion.help: Lions are Vulnerable: they've lost most of the land they once lived on.

facts: The biggest cat in the world.
No two tigers have the same stripes, and the stripes are on their skin too, not just their fur.
Unlike most cats, tigers love water and are strong swimmers.
tiger.help: Tigers are Endangered, but in India and Nepal their numbers are growing again thanks to rangers.

asian_elephant.home: Forests and grasslands in India and Southeast Asia.
facts: An elephant's trunk has tens of thousands of muscles. It can pick up a single peanut or a whole log.
Asian elephants have smaller ears than African elephants.
An adult eats about 150 kg (330 pounds) of plants a day.
asian_elephant.help: Asian elephants are Endangered. Forest corridors let herds travel safely.

red_panda.home: Misty bamboo forests high in the Himalaya mountains.
facts: Red pandas eat mostly bamboo, like giant pandas, but they aren't close relatives.
A long wrist bone works like an extra thumb for gripping bamboo.
In cold weather it wraps its fluffy striped tail round itself like a scarf.
red_panda.help: Red pandas are Endangered because their forests are being cut down.

black_rhino.home: Grasslands and bush in eastern and southern Africa.
facts: A black rhino has a pointed, hooked upper lip for grabbing leaves and twigs.
Its horn is made of keratin, the same stuff as your fingernails.
In 1995 only about 2,400 were left. Rangers have helped them more than double since.
black_rhino.help: Black rhinos are Critically Endangered. Rangers guard them day and night.

california_condor.home: Mountains and canyons of California, Arizona and Mexico.
facts: The biggest flying land bird in North America: its wings stretch almost 3 m (9.5 feet).
In 1987 only 27 were left, and all were brought in to be bred safely. Today there are more than 500, and over half fly free.
It can soar for hours on warm air without flapping.
california_condor.help: Condors are Critically Endangered. Lead-free hunting ammunition keeps them from being poisoned.

striped_skunk.home: Fields, woods and towns across North America.
facts: Before spraying, a skunk warns you: it stamps its feet, hisses and raises its tail.
Its spray can hit a target about 3 m (10 feet) away.
Skunks eat lots of grubs and insects, which helps gardens.

barn_owl.home: Farms, fields and old barns on every continent except Antarctica.
facts: Its heart-shaped face works like a satellite dish, steering sounds into its ears.
A barn owl can catch a mouse in total darkness, just by listening.
Soft, fringed feathers make its flight almost silent.

king_cobra.home: Rainforests and swamps in South and Southeast Asia.
facts: The longest venomous snake in the world: it can grow over 5 m (18 feet).
It can rear up a third of its body off the ground and still move forward.
It's the only snake that builds a nest for its eggs.
king_cobra.help: King cobras are Vulnerable as their forests shrink.

sumatran_orangutan.home: Rainforests on the island of Sumatra, in Indonesia.
facts: "Orangutan" means "person of the forest" in Malay.
Orangutans spend nearly all their lives in the trees, and build a fresh leafy nest to sleep in every night.
A baby stays with its mother for about 8 years, learning which fruits to eat.
sumatran_orangutan.help: Critically Endangered. Look for products made with sustainable palm oil.

harpy_eagle.home: Rainforests of Central and South America.
facts: Its back talons are about as long as a grizzly bear's claws.
It hunts sloths and monkeys high in the treetops.
When it's excited, the feathers on its head stand up like a crown.
harpy_eagle.help: Harpy eagles are Vulnerable: they need big, old rainforest trees to nest in.

hyacinth_macaw.home: Palm groves and wetlands in central South America.
facts: The biggest flying parrot in the world, about 1 m (3 feet) from beak to tail.
Its huge beak can crack palm nuts so hard that people need a hammer for them.
The bright yellow skin round its eyes and beak makes it look like it's smiling.
hyacinth_macaw.help: Hyacinth macaws are Vulnerable. Never buy wild-caught parrots.

wild_bactrian_camel.home: The Gobi Desert, in China and Mongolia.
facts: Its two humps store fat, not water, to live on when food is scarce.
It can drink salty water that most animals can't.
Fewer than about 1,000 are left in the wild.
wild_bactrian_camel.help: One of the rarest large mammals on Earth. Protected desert reserves keep them safe.

snapping_turtle.home: Ponds, rivers and marshes of North America.
facts: Its shell is too small to hide in, so it defends itself with a fast, strong bite.
In winter it can stay underwater under the ice for months.
Snapping turtles can live for more than 40 years.

honey_badger.home: Savannas, deserts and forests in Africa, the Middle East and India.
facts: Often called the most fearless animal in the world.
Its skin is thick and loose, so if something grabs it, it can twist round and bite back.
It breaks into beehives to eat the honey and the baby bees.

harbor_seal.home: Cool northern coasts of the Atlantic and Pacific oceans.
facts: Every harbor seal has its own pattern of spots.
Its whiskers can feel the trail of water left by a swimming fish, even in the dark.
It can stay underwater for up to about half an hour.
harbor_seal.help: Give seals resting on the beach plenty of space.

giant_panda.home: Bamboo forests in the mountains of central China.
facts: A giant panda spends up to 14 hours a day eating bamboo.
A newborn panda weighs only about 100 g, about as much as a stick of butter.
In 2016, pandas went from Endangered to Vulnerable thanks to new bamboo forest reserves.

mountain_gorilla.home: Misty mountain forests in Rwanda, Uganda and the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
facts: A big male, called a silverback, beats his chest to show off and talk to others.
Every gorilla's nose has its own shape, like a fingerprint.
Only about 1,000 are left, but rangers have helped their numbers grow.
mountain_gorilla.help: Mountain gorillas are Endangered. Old phones can be recycled so less coltan is mined in their forests.

komodo_dragon.home: A few islands in Indonesia, including Komodo.
facts: The biggest lizard in the world, up to 3 m (10 feet) long.
It smells with its forked tongue, tasting the air for food a long way off.
A female can lay eggs that hatch without a father.
komodo_dragon.help: Komodo dragons are Endangered as rising seas shrink their islands.

facts: Pangolins are the only mammals covered in scales, made of keratin like your fingernails.
When scared, it rolls into a tight, armored ball.
It eats ants and termites with a long, sticky tongue.
sunda_pangolin.help: Critically Endangered: pangolins are the most trafficked mammals in the world. Never buy pangolin products.

electric_eel.home: Rivers and swamps of the Amazon in South America.
facts: It isn't really an eel: it's a kind of knifefish.
One species can make a shock of up to 860 volts, the strongest of any animal.
It breathes air, coming up to the surface every few minutes.

pygmy_three_toed_sloth.home: The mangroves of one tiny island off Panama, Isla Escudo de Veraguas.
facts: The smallest sloth in the world, and one of the rarest mammals.
Sloths move so slowly that tiny green algae grow in their fur, helping them hide.
Slow on land, sloths are surprisingly good swimmers.
pygmy_three_toed_sloth.help: Critically Endangered. Protecting its island's mangroves is the only way to save it.

facts: In European stories, dragons breathe fire and guard heaps of treasure.
In China, dragons are wise and lucky, and bring the rain.

unicorn.home: Old stories from Europe and Asia.
facts: Stories of a horse with one horn go back more than 2,000 years.
The unicorn is Scotland's national animal.

yeti.home: Stories from the snowy Himalaya mountains of Nepal and Tibet.
facts: Mountaineers have photographed giant footprints in the snow and blamed the Yeti.
Local people tell many Yeti stories, and climbers have hunted for it for over 100 years.
In Greek myth, Cerberus guarded the gates of the underworld.
The hero Heracles had to capture him as the last of his twelve great labors.

kraken.home: Old sailors' stories from the seas off Norway.
facts: Sailors told of a sea monster big enough to pull ships under.
Real giant squid can grow as long as a bus, with eyes the size of dinner plates. One was first filmed alive in the deep sea in 2012.
